Unleash the hounds

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With an outstanding record of 145 arrests and 53 guns confiscated, we meet the K9 team making an incredible difference to the fight against rhino poaching in the Kruger National Park.

Unique Selling Point:
In 2017, Theresa Sowry, CEO of the South African Wildlife College, a wildlife training and management facility based near Kruger, visited dog trainer Joe Braman in Texas, USA. She had heard of his aggressive free-running pack dogs, Texas Coonhounds, used in law enforcement to track down escaped prisoners. While tracking dogs have been used in the Kruger before in the fight against rhino poaching, the animals were leashed and paired with human handlers. They were ultimately too slow to catch the poachers. But the Texas hounds operate very differently - they are sent after poachers unleashed, running in a pack, where they will signal the scent to each other in yips and yelps, and not stop until they've either caught their prey or run themselves into complete exhaustion. The pilot program currently running in the Kruger has had huge success with 145 arrests to date - a massive spike in the number of arrests since the program started running.

Summary:
Free-running pack hounds are a new and extremely useful tool in the anti-poaching arena, and the current pilot-program's successes speak for themselves. Except for the fact that the Texas hounds run unleashed, they have also been specifically trained to be aggressive, which normal scent dogs are not trained for. The Texas hounds have been taught to not only track down a poacher, but also attack, disarm and keep them at bay. The thinking is that a poacher, faced with a pack of attacking dogs, will drop his gun and climb a tree, giving law enforcement the chance to go in and make an arrest.

Further information:
The SAWC have agreed to allow us to film both training and a simulated tracking scenario. We have asked SANParks for permission, and also to provide their anti-poaching team, air support etc for the filming.

We have asked for permission to fly and film with a drone during our stay.

We will be staying over for one night at the SAWC, they are providing us rooms for free but we have to pay for meals. The closest other accommodation would be in Hoedspruit area, at least an hour's drive from where we want to be.



Extra Budget Items:
I have discussed using my vehicle for the trip with Wynand and Anna-Maria, as we need a large 4x4 for the trip. I will only charge my petrol money as used, with slips kept. This will be cheaper then renting a vehicle.

The problem is that it is a six hour drive from JHB to the SAWC. We are scheduled to film on monday and tuesday the 17th and 18th of February. To get the filming done we could leave JHB at 4am on the 17th, then film most of the afternoon and early evening as well as tuesday. The road, especially around Lydenburg, is notoriously bad and pot hole hell. It might be a good idea to sleep over on the tuesday night as well, and leave early wednesday morning. Flights to SKukuza Airport and car rental would be another option, but much more expensive. But WG must please advise.

Press Release:


Unleash the Hounds
They’ve fought them from the air, with specialised camouflage reconnaissance teams and tactical boots on the ground, but the latest weapon in the fight against rhino poaching might not be as high-tech as you would expect. Fast, four-legged and furious – free-tracking hounds could prove to be the game changer in the fight against poachers as they continue to achieve major successes in this deadly war.
Producer: Graham Coetzer | Research: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


Unleash the Hounds
First Draft Script
20 Feb 2020

Voice
The statistics are shocking… Over the past decade in excess of 8000 African rhinos have been lost to poaching. But now the innovative use of an age old technique might just make all the difference in the war to save an entire species.

Link Mac
Tracking dogs have played a major role in the continuing fight against rhino poaching, but the problem has always been that the animal, who is on a leash, can only move as fast as his human handler can. At the Southern African Wildlife College though, a new project is making a huge impact. And their secret? Unleashing the hounds…

Voice - On screen Title - DRAMATISATION
It’s early morning and the college’s K9 unit has been called into action - poachers have been spotted on a nearby reserve. A pack of hounds - a breed of dogs renowned for their hunting expertise - are rushed to an awaiting helicopter and airlifted to the poachers last known location. Once there, the dogs are unleashed to pick up the trail and chase down the suspects. Hunting down the scent faster and more effectively than any human ever could, the poachers are soon found and arrested. The footage you’ve just seen was a dramatisation, but college CEO Theresa Sowry says their hounds have achieved amazing successes in actual anti-poaching operations.

Sound Up Theresa Sowry
I can tell you through data that our unit collects, that using both on-lead and free running dogs, the percentage success rate increases from about 5 percent to about 68 percent if you combine canine assets.

Voice
She says the college was established in 1996 and has been supported amongst others by The Peace Parks Foundation to train wildlife area managers from across the SADC region in inclusive conservation. To date the College has trained over 17,000 people across 56 countries and 127 parks.

Sound Up Theresa
So the wildlife college tests best practice for conservation organisations, so that’s the lovely thing of working at an NGO and where we fundraise to test. We’re not an organisation that tries to push something on someone and say this works and this doesn’t, we’re allowed to test it and share in the good news. So what the college has been testing for a while now is our four-tiered approach to having greater success on the ground.

Voice
The first tier involves training rangers to world class standards.

Sound Up Theresa
So we’re always training new skills to field rangers, boots on the ground.

Link Mac
There really is an art to concealment, and when you’re surrounded by nature like this, the best weapon you have is to use nature itself. I think if you’re in a place like this you can… Hey!!!

Voice
Clive van Rooyen is the college’s Specialist Training manager, an ex-Task Force member whose job is, to provide rangers with advanced bush-craft skills.


Sound Up Clive
We teach them to basically disappear in the bush - that’s the easiest way to say it, and have the ability to affect arrests on criminal elements that enters the protected area.

Voice
The second tier includes the use of the free tracking hounds. Dog master Johan van Straaten is the man in charge of the K9 unit. Accompanied by Lola, his personal four legged companion, it’s van Straaten’s job to train the canine’s, keep them in peak physical condition and protect them during anti-poaching operations.

Sound Up Johan
Mac: So just please explain to me what is it that you do here at the Southern African Wildlife College?

Johan: Our main thing that we’re known of, is for the pack dogs, the high speed tracking dogs, that’s where we let go of a pack of dogs on a poacher’s tracks and we follow them with the chopper.

Voice
The unit’s dogs are not breed specific, and van Straaten and his team make use of a wide variety of canines, from Belgian Malinois to Beagles and of course the Hounds. Each breed has its own set of skills and certain breeds, like the malinois and beagles work better on-line, or on-leash, while the hounds are specifically chosen to work off-leash due to their high speed tracking abilities and pack mentality.

Sound Up Johan
So now with the pack dogs, the big benefit is about speed. They can go at a much faster pace than any line dog can ever do.

Voice
The unit has recently been bolstered by the donation of an additional twenty animals, trained to track down escaped convicts, all the way from Texas in the United States.

Sound Up Theresa
The Texans heard about us, and Jo Braman, via the Ivan Carter Wildlife Conservation Alliance, donated twenty of their dogs from Texas for us to integrate, and for us to learn from Texas to run our dogs.

Voice
We got to join the K9 team during an early morning training exercise.

Link Mac
So what they’re doing now is fitting the GPS trackers, if you see there’s a little antennae on all of the dogs there.

Voice
The tracking collars help the team to know the exact whereabouts of every single dog during live operations.

Sound Up Johan
The dogs get confidence from each other. So when they’re on tracks, they’ve got the back up of the rest of the pack. And there is a little bit of competition going on between them, and that brings up the speed, which is what it’s all about.

Voice
Training exercises like these take place in Big Five territory, so the canines are taught to ignore and avoid live game, and only focus on tracking human scents.

Sound Up Teresa
We are in a very unique and privileged position where the college is actually based on a contractual national park, just outside the Kruger National Park.

Voice
That’s one of the reasons the K9’s always have air support during live operations.

Sound Up Teresa
And we stick with our dogs to make sure that they don’t run into harms way, be it poachers or be it other animals.

Voice
Back in the bush two rather brave rangers had volunteered to play the role of our poachers. Armed with a dog bite suit and their own gps tracker, the men set off to go and hide.

Sound Up Johan
So we’re going to see how long it takes the track-layers to lay the track, and then when the dogs are doing the track we’ll see how fast the dogs do the track.

Link Mac
As you can see they are quite excited, they can’t wait to get out of there, and hopefully be able to find them. So it’s going to be quite interesting to see what they do, how they get out and how they follow that spoor.

Voice
And then, with Johan in place to indicate the scent to the pack, finally, the release.

Sound Up Dogs Release

Voice
The hounds picked up the trail almost instantly, and the chase was on.

Sound Up Johan
Johan: So whenever the hounds are on the track they will open up and they will howl, they will bark on the track.

Mac: Yes.

Johan: And that keeps the communication between the dogs together. And the moment they lose the track, they will all keep quiet, and they will split up, and each dog will start looking for the tracks.

Mac: So they’re busy, they’re sniffing, they’re looking for this…

Johan: Everyone is doing their own type of thing. And the first dog that finds the track will open up, wooo, and the other dogs will honour that bark.

Voice
And as we saw from the air, the pack will once again resume their hunt.

Sound Up Johan
Johan: So you can see all the dogs, all their names are their, they are running as a pack, they’re all together, and the dogs are running on the track layers track, you can see they are exactly following that track.

Mac: There we go.

Johan: And they are almost there, they started at five minutes past seven, so they’ve done it in two minutes and the guys walked for 10 minutes.

Mac: Oh that’s brilliant.

Johan: So that’s why we call it high speed tracking dogs.

Voice
In real world operations poachers will often climb trees to evade the hounds, and be loathe to shoot at them to avoid firefights with law enforcement

Link Mac
So our mock poachers took about ten minutes to get to the place where they are, it took the dogs two minutes. They worked as a pack, they went really really fast.

Voice
A key part of the training is for the hounds to receive rewards for a job well done, in this case it’s the praise of their handlers and the joy of catching their prey. The hounds are not encouraged to attack, only to keep poachers at bay, and at Johan’s command the pack stands down.

Link Mac
After a hard day’s work it’s always nice to have a cold one, and in this case a bit of water. After action, satisfaction.

Voice
For rangers like Kelly Nendouvhada, who left a career in banking to study at the college before becoming one of their trainers, applied learning makes all the difference in the fight for conservation. This means that it not just about theory, the students at the College learn by doing.

Sound Up Kelly
Remember that we are based in Kruger National Park, chances of encountering the real poachers is very high. Instilling that knowledge in them, to say guys we are in the real Kruger, we are in the real places where the real poachers can actually come.

Voice
For ground teams to be successful, they need air support, which makes up the third tier. Pilot Bruce McDonald trains rangers in ground to air communication and bush flying, while his light sports aircraft provides a birds eye-view of animals or poachers on the ground.

Sound Up Theresa
While we’re flying we’re actually monitoring the asset. We’re able to tell the rangers on the ground exactly where the asset is.

Voice
The fourth and final tier involves getting local communities to buy into the conservation drive. One of project leader Sboniso Phakhati’s current initiatives involves teaching youngsters to use survival techniques animals have developed in the wild, to give them the edge in everyday human activities.

Sound Up Sboniso
Really the aim of this program is to inspire kids who care, who care for themselves, who care for each other, and who care for the environment around them. And this is just a brilliant way to infuse sport and conservation learning.



Voice
South Africa is home to nearly 80% of the world’s rhino’s, and has been the country, hardest hit by poaching syndicates. For the men, women and canines of the Southern African Wildlife College, the hope is to roll out their unique approach to game parks all over the SADC region in the near future.

Sound Up Theresa
So boots on the ground, then free-tracking dogs, aerial surveillance and community beneficiation allows for a much better success story.












Promo 1
Voice
The latest weapon in the fight against rhino poaching might not be as hi-tech as you would expect - but packs of free tracking hounds are achieving major successes in the ongoing war against rhino poaching.

Promo 2
Voice
They’re fast, four legged and furious - free tracking hounds are proving to be game changers in the fight back against rhino poachers. Could this be the ultimate solution to ending the poaching epidemic?

Promo 3
Voice
The Southern African Wildlife College is using a multi-levelled approach to stop rhino poachers in their tracks - while achieving unheard of successes in the field. Their secret?… Unleashing the hounds….

Sound Up Dogs Release

Mac: So they’re busy, they’re sniffing, they’re looking for this… Johan: Everyone is doing their own type of thing. And the first dog that finds the track will open up, wooo, and the other dogs will honour that bark. Voice And as we saw from the air, the pack will once again resume their hunt. Sound Up Johan Johan: So you can see all the dogs, all their names are their, they are running as a pack, they’re all together, and the dogs are running on the track layers track, you can see they are exactly following that track. Mac: There we go. Johan: And they are almost there, they started at five minutes past seven, so they’ve done it in two minutes and the guys walked for 10 minutes. Mac: Oh that’s brilliant. Johan: So that’s why we call it high speed tracking dogs. Voice In real world operations poachers will often climb trees to evade the hounds, and be loathe to shoot at them to avoid firefights with law enforcement Link Mac So our mock poachers took about ten minutes to get to the place where they are, it took the dogs two minutes. They worked as a pack, they went really really fast. Voice A key part of the training is for the hounds to receive rewards for a job well done, in this case it’s the praise of their handlers and the joy of catching their prey. The hounds are not encouraged to attack, only to keep poachers at bay, and at Johan’s command the pack stands down. Link Mac After a hard day’s work it’s always nice to have a cold one, and in this case a bit of water. After action, satisfaction. Voice For rangers like Kelly Nendouvhada, who left a career in banking to study at the college before becoming one of their trainers, applied learning makes all the difference in the fight for conservation. This means that it not just about theory, the students at the College learn by doing. Sound Up Kelly Remember that we are based in Kruger National Park, chances of encountering the real poachers is very high. Instilling that knowledge in them, to say guys we are in the real Kruger, we are in the real places where the real poachers can actually come. Voice For ground teams to be successful, they need air support, which makes up the third tier. Pilot Bruce McDonald trains rangers in ground to air communication and bush flying, while his light sports aircraft provides a birds eye-view of animals or poachers on the ground. Sound Up Theresa While we’re flying we’re actually monitoring the asset. We’re able to tell the rangers on the ground exactly where the asset is. Voice The fourth and final tier involves getting local communities to buy into the conservation drive. One of project leader Sboniso Phakhati’s current initiatives involves teaching youngsters to use survival techniques animals have developed in the wild, to give them the edge in everyday human activities. Sound Up Sboniso Really the aim of this program is to inspire kids who care, who care for themselves, who care for each other, and who care for the environment around them. And this is just a brilliant way to infuse sport and conservation learning. Voice South Africa is home to nearly 80% of the world’s rhino’s, and has been the country, hardest hit by poaching syndicates. For the men, women and canines of the Southern African Wildlife College, the hope is to roll out their unique approach to game parks all over the SADC region in the near future. Sound Up Theresa So boots on the ground, then free-tracking dogs, aerial surveillance and community beneficiation allows for a much better success story. Promo 1 Voice The latest weapon in the fight against rhino poaching might not be as hi-tech as you would expect - but packs of free tracking hounds are achieving major successes in the ongoing war against rhino poaching. Promo 2 Voice They’re fast, four legged and furious - free tracking hounds are proving to be game changers in the fight back against rhino poachers. Could this be the ultimate solution to ending the poaching epidemic? Promo 3 Voice The Southern African Wildlife College is using a multi-levelled approach to stop rhino poachers in their tracks - while achieving unheard of successes in the field. Their secret?… Unleashing the hounds…. Sound Up Dogs Release

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With an outstanding record of 145 arrests and 53 guns confiscated, we meet the K9 team making an incredible difference to the fight against rhino poaching in the Kruger National Park.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In 2017, Theresa Sowry, CEO of the South African Wildlife College, a wildlife training and management facility based near Kruger, visited dog trainer Joe Braman in Texas, USA. She had heard of his aggressive free-running pack dogs, Texas Coonhounds, used in law enforcement to track down escaped prisoners. While tracking dogs have been used in the Kruger before in the fight against rhino poaching, the animals were leashed and paired with human handlers. They were ultimately too slow to catch the poachers. But the Texas hounds operate very differently - they are sent after poachers unleashed, running in a pack, where they will signal the scent to each other in yips and yelps, and not stop until they've either caught their prey or run themselves into complete exhaustion. The pilot program currently running in the Kruger has had huge success with 145 arrests to date - a massive spike in the number of arrests since the program started running.
metadata.Summary: Free-running pack hounds are a new and extremely useful tool in the anti-poaching arena, and the current pilot-program's successes speak for themselves. Except for the fact that the Texas hounds run unleashed, they have also been specifically trained to be aggressive, which normal scent dogs are not trained for. The Texas hounds have been taught to not only track down a poacher, but also attack, disarm and keep them at bay. The thinking is that a poacher, faced with a pack of attacking dogs, will drop his gun and climb a tree, giving law enforcement the chance to go in and make an arrest.
metadata.Further information: The SAWC have agreed to allow us to film both training and a simulated tracking scenario.
